qs.q: A newborn is diagnosed with an omphalocele characterized by an epigastric defect, a diaphragmatic defect, a pericardial defect, a short lower sternum, and an intracardiac defect. What is this syndrome called?
qs.e: Pentalogy of Cantrell consists of an epigastric omphalocele, a diaphragmatic defect, pericardial defect, split or short lower sternum and an intracardiac defect. Beckwith-Wiedemann involves macroglossia and hypoglycaemia.

qs.q: A 24-year-old Kenyan man develops a firm, raised dermal lesion on his sternum six months after sustaining a minor chest wall injury. The lesion clearly extends well beyond the original boundaries of the initial trauma site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Keloids grow beyond the margins of the original wound and rarely regress, particularly in dark-skinned individuals on the sternum. Hypertrophic scars stay within the original wound boundaries and often regress over time.

qs.q: Which muscle originates from the medial half of the clavicle, sternum, and upper costal cartilages, and acts to adduct and medially rotate the arm?
qs.e: Pectoralis major originates from the medial clavicle, sternum, and upper costal cartilages, inserting to move the arm via medial and lateral pectoral nerve innervation. Pectoralis minor inserts on the coracoid process instead.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The sternum is the central flat bone of the anterior thorax, anchoring ribs and protecting the heart. Its shape and relations guide clinical assessment of chest trauma and cardiac imaging.

sections.p: The sternum is a flat, midline bone that forms the front of the thoracic cage. It provides attachment for ribs and protects vital organs such as the heart and great vessels.
b: Divided into manubrium, body, xiphoid process

sections.p: It lies anterior to the heart, extending from the jugular notch to the xiphoid process. The manubrium articulates with the clavicles and first ribs; the body with the second to seventh ribs; the xiphoid is cartilaginous in youth.
b: Manubrium: jugular notch to sternal angle

sections.p: Posteriorly the sternum lies against the sternocostal joints and the pericardium. It is adjacent to the heart’s apex and base, the great vessels, and the trachea.
b: Heart apex at 5th intercostal space left
Sternal angle (Angle of Louis) marks T4–T5 junction

sections.p: The sternum receives arterial blood from the internal thoracic (mammary) arteries and the superior epigastric arteries.
Innervation is via the intercostal nerves (T2–T6) and the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) for diaphragmatic reflexes.
It protects the heart and great vessels, provides attachment for ribs and muscles, and contributes to the thoracic cage’s structural integrity.
Fractures, especially of the manubrium or xiphoid, can indicate high-energy trauma and may compromise cardiac function. Osteomyelitis or metastatic disease can involve the sternum.
b: Manubrial fractures suggest severe chest trauma
Xiphoid fractures common in forceful vomiting

t.b: Shows fracture lines or displacement; abnormal if sternal edges are misaligned
Defines fracture extent and adjacent organ injury; abnormal if bone fragments impinge on heart or vessels

sections.p: When assessing chest pain, palpate the sternum for tenderness. A sternal angle at the 4th rib indicates normal anatomy; deviation may signal rib fractures or scoliosis.
Treat underlying cause: fracture stabilization, infection control, or tumor resection. Supportive care includes pain control, respiratory support, and monitoring for cardiac compromise.
Sternal fractures can mimic costochondritis or myocardial infarction pain.
In low‑resource settings, a normal chest X‑ray may miss a subtle sternal fracture; clinical correlation is essential.
b: Subtle fractures may be radiographically occult

whenToSeekHelp: Severe chest pain with sternal tenderness, dyspnea, or signs of cardiac tamponade

faq.q: What is the sternal angle used for?
faq.a: It marks the junction of the manubrium and body and aligns with the 4th rib, useful for locating heart structures.

faq.q: Can the sternum fracture in a fall?
faq.a: Yes, especially the manubrium in high‑energy impacts; xiphoid fractures can occur with forceful vomiting.

faq.q: Is the sternum a good site for bone marrow donation?
faq.a: In adults, the sternum contains active marrow and can be used for bone marrow harvest when other sites are unsuitable.
